2 mega-cap stocks with exciting potential and 1 we avoid

Megacap stocks dominate their sectors and their actions influence economies worldwide. The flip side though is that their sheer size means they have less room for explosive growth as scale works against them.

Sound complicated? With StockStory, it doesn't have to be. Our job is to find you high-quality companies that can win regardless of the conditions. Keeping that in mind, here are two industry titans with attractive long-term potential and one that could be stalling.

One mega-cap stock to sell:
Walmart (WMT)

Market cap: $962 billion

Known for its large-format Supercenters, Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) is a retail pioneer that serves a budget-conscious consumer who is looking for a wide range of products under one roof.

Why Are We Wary of WMT?

The company has faced growth challenges as its 5.3% annual revenue increases over the last three years fell short of other consumer retail companies

Widely-available products (and therefore stiff competition) result in an inferior gross margin of 24.9% that must be offset through higher volumes

Responsiveness to unforeseen market trends is restricted due to its substandard operating margin profitability

Walmart's stock price of $123.24 implies a valuation ratio of 39.5x forward P/E. If you're considering WMT for your portfolio, see our FREE research report to learn more.

Two mega-cap stocks to watch:
Microsoft (MSFT)

Market cap: $3.94 trillion

Originally named "Micro-soft" for microcomputer software when founded in 1975, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) is a global technology company that develops software, cloud services, devices, and AI solutions for consumers, businesses, and organizations worldwide.

Why Should You Buy MSFT?

Microsoft is one of the great brands not just in tech but all of business. It produces mission-critical software and bundles it together, resulting in cream-of-the-crop gross margins.

The company's elite unit economics lead to robust profit margins that improve over time. This speaks to the scale advantages and operating efficiency across its diverse portfolio, which spans everything from Office and Azure to Minecraft.

Microsoft has a virtuous cycle of returns. Its dominant market position enables it to generate strong free cash flow, and it reinvests these funds into promising ventures that further strengthen its competitive moat.

title: Adobe Drops 29% YTD: Should You Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock?

Adobe Drops 29% YTD: Should You Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock?
Aniruddha Ganguly

MSFT
GOOG
CRM
OPAI.PVT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Adobe ADBE shares have dropped 29.1% year to date (YTD), underperforming the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector's return of 17.5%. The weakness appears to reflect investor concerns over intensifying competition from AI-native creative platforms, uncertainty surrounding AI monetization, modest recurring revenue growth, pressure on profitability and leadership transition risks.

The company has been playing a catch-up role in the AI domain, not only against established players like Microsoft MSFT, Alphabet GOOGL and Salesforce CRM, but also from AI-native companies like OpenAI, Midjourney and Canva. YTD, Adobe shares have underperformed Alphabet's 9.3% drop, Salesforce's decline of 12.8% and Microsoft's appreciation of 9.7%. So, what should investors do with Adobe stock? Let's find out.

ADBE Stock's Price Performance
Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Adobe Faces Multiple Challenges

The rapid proliferation of AI-powered content creation tools is challenging Adobe's traditional competitive advantages in creative software. AI-native platforms capable of generating images, videos, designs and marketing content through natural-language prompts are reducing dependence on traditional creative applications such as Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere. Adobe is responding by embedding conversational AI and autonomous creative agents into its flagship applications. However, investors remain concerned that generative AI could commoditize certain creative workflows, increase pricing pressure and weaken ADBE's ability to sustain premium subscription pricing.

Meanwhile, AI-first ending Annualized Recurring Revenue (ARR) exceeded $650 million and surged more than 150% year over year. AI-first offerings still represent a relatively small portion of the overall recurring revenue base. Adobe expects ARR growth of 10.2% by the end of fiscal 2026, suggesting that strong adoption of new AI offerings has yet to meaningfully accelerate companywide recurring revenue growth. Investors have been skeptical about how quickly increasing usage of Firefly, AI Assistant and agentic workflows will translate into sustained revenue acceleration.

Adobe expects fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 revenues between $6.80 billion and $6.85 billion, implying approximately 1% sequential growth at the midpoint. The guidance suggests relatively modest near-term sequential revenue momentum despite rapidly growing AI engagement. Adobe also projects a non-GAAP operating margin of approximately 44% for the fiscal fourth quarter, below its fiscal 2026 target of approximately 45%. Continued investments in AI infrastructure, product development and customer acquisition could constrain margin expansion over the near term.

title: Big Tech Stocks Have Never Looked Cheaper. Is the Magnificent Seven a Screaming Buy?
detail:
Big Tech Stocks Have Never Looked Cheaper. Is the Magnificent Seven a Screaming Buy?
Jeremy Bowman, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 1:20 PM EDT 4 min read
^IXIC
AMZN
NVDA
INTC
SNDK
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Following another sell-off in tech stocks, the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) is now on the verge of a correction as the index is down roughly 8% from its closing peak.

On Friday, the trigger was underwhelming earnings reports from a slew of tech companies like Amazon, Intel, and Sandisk, offering the latest evidence that investors have grown weary with the AI trade.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Amazon joined its hyperscaler peers like Alphabet, Microsoft, and Meta Platforms in falling in response to earnings, a sign that investors have become skeptical of the massive capital spending taking place in the cloud computing industry. Combined, these four companies are set to spend more than $700 billion this year. The world has never seen an infrastructure build-out of that size.

Though these stocks have all fallen this earnings season, their profits continue to grow, meaning many of them are as cheap as they've ever been. All four hyperscalers are reporting record profits, and, except for Microsoft, they're all trading at substantial discounts from their recent peaks.

AMZN data by YCharts

How cheap are the hyperscalers?

Assessing the valuation of these stocks isn't so easy. With the exception of Microsoft, they don't adjust their earnings to reflect one-time events, so reported earnings per share doesn't offer a clear picture of profits. Alphabet and Amazon, for example, both made large gains in their investments in Anthropic this year.

If we use operating income instead, we can get a better sense of their valuations.

AMZN EBIT (TTM) data by YCharts

Combined, these companies had roughly $490 billion in operating income in the last year, including Amazon's most recent quarter. Their total market cap is now $11.5 trillion, meaning they trade altogether at 23.5 times operating income, which is similar to the S&P 500.

Image source: Getty Images.

Why are big tech stocks so cheap?

The simple explanation for why these stocks have gotten so cheap is that all four of these, except Microsoft, are now burning cash to fund their AI build-outs, and investors have gotten spooked by the risk in that investment.

AMZN Free Cash Flow (Quarterly) data by YCharts

Updated for the third quarter, Amazon's free cash flow dropped to a loss of $34.8 billion.

Even though three out of four of these stocks have large, highly profitable cloud computing businesses that can monetize that spend, the AI industry is still new, and long-term demand is uncertain.

title: GOOGL Drops 13% Post Q3 Earnings: Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock?
detail:
GOOGL Drops 13% Post Q3 Earnings: Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock?
Aniruddha Ganguly

GOOG
AMZN
AAPL
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Alphabet GOOGL shares plunged 12.64% on Thursday, following the release of third-quarter 2026 results, wiping out $482 billion in market capitalization. The selloff reflected concerns over slowing Google Search advertising growth, weaker monetization of AI-powered searches, mounting AI infrastructure expenditures, negative free cash flow and disappointing earnings. Although Alphabet delivered 25% year-over-year revenue growth and Google Cloud revenues more than doubled, investors questioned whether the company's massive AI investments would generate sufficient returns to offset pressure on its core advertising business. Let's dig deep to find out.

GOOGL Stock Suffers From Multiple Challenges

Google Search and other advertising revenues increased 12% year over year to $63.35 billion in the third quarter, decelerating from approximately 17% growth in the second quarter. The revenue figure also missed the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 2.53%. This slowdown was particularly concerning because Search remains Alphabet's largest revenue contributor and provides significant cash flows to fund AI investments. GOOGL acknowledged that growing AI Mode usage contributed to Search revenue deceleration because AI Mode queries currently generate lower monetization than traditional searches.

Alphabet's capital expenditures surged 114% year over year to $51.36 billion in the third quarter of 2026, exceeding operating cash flow of $42.29 billion. Consequently, free cash flow deteriorated to negative $9.07 billion from positive $24.46 billion a year earlier. Trailing 12-month free cash flow declined 73% year over year to $19.75 billion. Alphabet maintained its 2026 capital expenditure guidance of $195-$205 billion and expects spending to increase significantly in 2027.

Meanwhile, the company's aggressive AI expansion is increasing its financial obligations. At the end of September 2026, GOOGL reported approximately $924 billion in future purchase commitments and $152 billion in pre-commencement leases and other obligations, representing more than $1 trillion in maximum contractual commitments. Alphabet cautioned that flexible pricing and volume terms could reduce actual spending. Long-term debt increased to $125.1 billion from $46.5 billion at the end of 2025. Alphabet also raised approximately $12.4 billion through common stock issuance during the third quarter and $28.7 billion through senior unsecured notes.

Apart from risks associated with the huge AI-related capital expenditure, Alphabet's prospects suffer from intensifying competition from the likes of Microsoft MSFT, Amazon AMZN, OpenAI, Anthropic, Apple AAPL and Meta across its operational footprint. Year to date (YTD), Alphabet shares have dropped 9.3%, underperforming Apple's 28.4%, Microsoft's 9.7% and Amazon's 5.7% returns.
